Miss Petowker arrives to join the Crummles company and secretly marries the elderly Mr. Lillyvick in a farcically theatrical wedding ceremony, while Nicholas patiently coaches Smike for his stage debut as the Apothecary in Romeo and Juliet.

Sir Mulberry Hawk and Lord Verisopht pressure Ralph Nickleby into revealing Kate's address so they can pursue her, while Mrs. Nickleby's chance visit to Ralph's house lets the two rakes extract even more information about Kate under the guise of flattery.

Sir Mulberry Hawk's toadies Pyke and Pluck flatter Mrs. Nickleby into attending the theatre, where Hawk maneuvers to isolate Kate and harass her, while her oblivious mother mistakes Kate's distress for signs of love.

Kate Nickleby, relentlessly persecuted by Sir Mulberry Hawk during his visits to the Wititterly household, finally confronts Ralph Nickleby and begs him to intervene, but Ralph coldly refuses on business grounds, leaving Kate to depart in tears while Newman Noggs offers silent sympathy.

Nicholas earns twenty pounds from a benefit performance, sends money to Kate via Newman Noggs, defends himself against a theatrical rival (Lenville) who challenges him to a humiliating confrontation, knocks Lenville down and forces an apology, then receives a cryptic warning letter from Newman hinting that Kate may soon need her brother's protection.

Nicholas bids farewell to the Crummles troupe with staged "last appearances" and a rowdy supper party, then abruptly quits Portsmouth with Smike after an urgent letter from Newman Noggs summons him back to London.

Newman Noggs, after spying on Ralph and running an errand, visits Miss La Creevy to reveal Ralph's mistreatment of Kate and plan how to carefully break the news to the returning Nicholas without provoking reckless violence.

Nicholas returns to London with Smike, discovers Kate's situation is alarming, overhears Sir Mulberry Hawk and companions mock Kate at a hotel, confronts Hawk demanding his name, and the standoff erupts into a violent carriage struggle in which Nicholas wounds Hawk with a whip handle before being flung to the ground.

After fighting Sir Mulberry Hawk, Nicholas rescues Kate from the Wititterly household, evacuates his mother from Ralph's lodgings, and delivers a letter to Ralph severing all family ties in condemnation of his villainy.

Ralph Nickleby meets Mantalini to discount bills and witnesses his comic marital skirmish, then receives Squeers who reports Nicholas's attack on Sir Mulberry Hawk, prompting Ralph and Squeers to conspire against Nicholas by using the abandoned boy (Smike) as a weapon.

Nicholas introduces Smike to his mother and Kate, then encounters the philanthropic Cheeryble Brothers at a register office, who immediately hire him as a clerk and arrange cheap lodgings, restoring the Nickleby family to modest happiness.

Nicholas visits the Kenwigs household during Mrs. Kenwigs's confinement and delivers the devastating news that Mr. Lillyvick has married Miss Petowker, destroying the family's hopes of inheriting his fortune.

Nicholas wins Tim Linkinwater's approval as a clerk at Cheeryble Brothers and attends their annual birthday dinner, then returns home where Mrs. Nickleby confides that their eccentric next-door neighbour has been tossing vegetables over the garden wall as love-tokens and has proposed marriage to her.

Smike is ambushed and seized on the London streets by Squeers and his son and locked up at Snawley's lodgings, while Ralph Nickleby visits the bedridden Sir Mulberry Hawk and deliberately fans his rage for revenge against Nicholas.

John Browdie, visiting London with his new wife and Fanny Squeers, learns that Squeers has recaptured Smike; he feigns illness to get upstairs unattended, then frees Smike from the locked room and sends him running home before Squeers can notice.

Smike flees Squeers and is sheltered by Newman Noggs before being reunited with Nicholas and Kate; meanwhile Nicholas becomes obsessively infatuated with a mysterious young woman glimpsed at the Cheeryble brothers' office, enlists Newman as go-between, and the clandestine meeting ends in farce when Newman has followed the wrong servant to entirely the wrong girl.

Mrs. Nickleby and Kate are pelted with vegetables and propositioned by their eccentric mad neighbor who scales the garden wall; Kate is alarmed, but Mrs. Nickleby, flattered, half-believes his extravagant declarations are genuine courtship until his keeper drags him down and reveals him as a long-mad, wicked old man.

Nicholas dines with John and Tilly Browdie, who recount how John helped Smike escape from Squeers, until Squeers and his daughter Fanny burst in and berate the Browdies and Nicholas before storming out in theatrical fury.

Nicholas meets Frank Cheeryble by chance at an inn after a brawl, they are formally introduced at the counting-house next morning, and Frank accompanies his uncle Charles on a warm visit to the Nickleby cottage — ending with Smike collapsing alone in silent bitter grief.

Ralph coldly rebuffs his returned-convict former clerk Brooker who claims a secret hold over him, then witnesses Madame Mantalini publicly renounce her husband and cede the business to Miss Knag, before departing covertly with Squeers and an unknown third man—an exit that alarms Newman Noggs.

Ralph Nickleby arrives at the Nickleby cottage with Squeers and Snawley, who presents documents claiming to be Smike's father and demands his return, but Nicholas refuses to surrender Smike despite the seemingly valid legal claim, and Ralph departs with threats of legal ruin.

Cheeryble Brothers commission Nicholas to secretly support Madeline Bray by posing as an art buyer, and on his first visit he silently falls in love with her while enduring her father's petulant pride — all while Ralph Nickleby's earlier attempt to poison the brothers against Nicholas is rebuffed.

Ralph Nickleby and elderly moneylender Arthur Gride secretly conspire to coerce imprisoned debtor Walter Bray into pressuring his daughter Madeline into marriage with Gride, while Newman Noggs eavesdrops from a closet and is horrified by the scheme.

Nicholas, brooding over his hopeless love for Madeline Bray, stumbles upon a playbill announcing Vincent Crummles's last London appearance, reunites with the troupe, attends their farewell supper, and debates the ethics of dramatic adaptation before bidding the Crummles family goodbye as they depart for America.

While Smike's health visibly deteriorates and Kate's feelings for Frank Cheeryble grow, the Nickleby household is comically disrupted when the mad neighbor in small-clothes descends the chimney, convinced Miss La Creevy is his beloved.

At a Hampton race-course gambling den, Sir Mulberry Hawk and Lord Frederick Verisopht quarrel over Sir Mulberry's vowed revenge against Nicholas (aided by Ralph Nickleby's intelligence), come to blows, fight a pistol duel at dawn, and Lord Frederick is shot dead while Sir Mulberry flees to France.

Newman Noggs, carrying a letter between Ralph Nickleby and miser Arthur Gride, secretly reads it and discovers the imminent plot to marry Madeline Bray to Gride, then urgently reveals the scheme to Nicholas, who storms off in fury to stop it.

Nicholas despairs over Madeline Bray's imminent forced marriage but, rallied by Newman Noggs, resolves to appeal to her directly; meanwhile Newman escorts young Morleena Kenwigs to a barber, where they encounter the humbled Mr. Lillyvick, who reveals his wife eloped with a captain and, reconciled with the Kenwigs family, pledges to settle his fortune on their children.
Nicholas makes a desperate last appeal to Madeline to postpone her marriage to Gride, then confronts Gride directly, but both efforts fail and the wedding remains set for the following morning.

On Madeline Bray's wedding morning, Nicholas and Kate burst in to offer her refuge; Bray dies suddenly before the ceremony can proceed, and Nicholas seizes the moment to carry the unconscious Madeline away, defeating Ralph and Gride's scheme.

While Madeline Bray recovers from dangerous illness under Kate's nursing and Mrs. Nickleby schemes around Frank Cheeryble's suspected love for Kate, Nicholas firmly rejects any encouragement of the match out of honour toward the brothers; Smike's consumption then worsens critically and Nicholas departs with him to Devonshire, parting from Kate in a sorrowful farewell.

Ralph Nickleby, seething after Nicholas foiled Gride's marriage scheme and learning of a financial ruin, dismisses Newman Noggs and recruits Squeers to steal a deed proving Madeline's inheritance, planning to destroy it and defeat Nicholas.

Squeers, operating as Ralph Nickleby's agent, plies the deaf housekeeper Peg Sliderskew with drink to examine stolen documents she took from Arthur Gride, pockets a deed naming Madeline Bray, then is knocked senseless by Newman Noggs while Frank Cheeryble looks on.

Nicholas tends the dying Smike at their childhood home, where Smike sees a terrifying vision of the man who first brought him to Dotheboys Hall, then peacefully dies after confessing his secret love for Kate Nickleby.

Ralph Nickleby, sleepless and increasingly paranoid, discovers his co-conspirators Snawley and Squeers have been arrested or turned against him, and is finally confronted at the Cheeryble Brothers' office by Newman Noggs—who reveals he exposed the plot—and by the brothers themselves, who lay out the full evidence of Ralph's scheme against Smike and warn him to flee before justice falls.

Brooker confesses to the Cheeryble Brothers that Smike — whom Ralph persecuted to death — was Ralph's own secret son, placed at Dotheboys Hall under a false name; Ralph, shattered by the revelation, flees into the night.

Nicholas returns home after Smike's death, confesses his secret love for Madeline to Kate (who has likewise refused Frank Cheeryble's proposal out of duty), then visits brother Charles to disclose his feelings and beg that Madeline be removed from his household, learning that a meeting with Ralph Nickleby has been arranged.
Ralph Nickleby, broken by the revelation that Smike was his own son and that all his schemes have collapsed, returns home in anguish and hangs himself in the garret.

The Cheeryble Brothers reveal Madeline's rightful inheritance has been recovered and orchestrate betrothals — Nicholas to Madeline, Frank to Kate — while Tim Linkinwater proposes to Miss La Creevy and a transformed Newman Noggs reappears, all celebrated at a triumphant dinner.

Nicholas travels to Yorkshire to share his good fortune with John Browdie, stumbles upon the degraded Mantalini grinding a mangle in a London cellar, then witnesses news of Squeers's transportation trigger a full pupil revolt at Dotheboys Hall, which empties and closes forever.

The concluding chapter resolves all fates: Nicholas weds Madeline and joins the Cheeryble firm, Kate marries Frank Cheeryble, the villains (Ralph, Squeers, Hawk, Gride) meet ruin or death, Newman Noggs retires contentedly near Nicholas's household, and Smike's grave is tended by Nicholas's children.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/Oliver_Twist/Chap.plot: Oliver Twist is born in a workhouse to an unknown woman who dies moments after childbirth, leaving him a nameless pauper orphan with no known origin.

On Oliver's ninth birthday Mr. Bumble collects him from Mrs. Mann's farm and delivers him to the workhouse board, where a starvation regime finally drives Oliver to ask for more gruel, earning him confinement and an offer of five pounds to any master willing to take him as apprentice.

After a week in solitary confinement, Oliver is nearly apprenticed to Gamfield, a brutal chimney-sweep, but a magistrate notices Oliver's terror and refuses to sign the indentures, returning him to the workhouse.
The parish board apprentices Oliver to undertaker Sowerberry; Mr Bumble delivers him there, where he is fed dog scraps and bedded among coffins.

Oliver, apprenticed to undertaker Sowerberry, endures bullying from charity-boy Noah Claypole, then accompanies his master and Mr Bumble to a pauper's funeral where he witnesses a starved woman's hasty, perfunctory burial and the grief of her destitute family.

Goaded past endurance when Noah Claypole slanders his dead mother, Oliver violently attacks him, is subdued and locked in the dust-cellar by the Sowerberry household, and Noah is dispatched to fetch Mr. Bumble.

After Noah's false complaint brings Mr Bumble, Oliver defiantly refuses to be cowed, endures beating and confinement, then at dawn escapes the undertaker's and bids farewell to his dying workhouse friend Dick before fleeing into the open road.
After a week-long starving journey on foot, Oliver reaches Barnet where he meets the Artful Dodger, who leads him into London's slums and delivers him to Fagin's criminal den.
Oliver wakes in Fagin's den, secretly watches Fagin gloat over hidden stolen jewels, then witnesses and is taught pickpocketing tricks by the Dodger and Charley Bates while Nancy briefly visits.
Oliver accompanies the Dodger and Charley Bates on their first "job," witnesses them pick Mr Brownlow's pocket, flees in panic, and is seized by the crowd and a police officer as the presumed thief.

Oliver is dragged before the bullying magistrate Mr. Fang, nearly condemned despite Mr. Brownlow's doubts, then discharged when a bookseller witness proves his innocence; fainting from illness, Oliver is carried away in a coach by Mr. Brownlow.

Oliver convalesces at Mr Brownlow's house under Mrs Bedwin's care until Brownlow notices Oliver's face exactly matches a mysterious portrait on the wall, while the Artful Dodger and Charley Bates flee back to Fagin after abandoning Oliver during the pickpocketing arrest.

Fagin and Bill Sikes learn Oliver has been taken away by a benefactor after being cleared of theft; they coerce Nancy into infiltrating the police office to locate him, and she discovers Oliver is gone to Pentonville, prompting Fagin to order the gang to find and recapture him.

Oliver recuperates at Mr Brownlow's house, enjoys kindness and new clothes, then is sent on an errand to return books and pay a debt — an act Mr Grimwig bets he will never complete — and fails to return as darkness falls.

Nancy, coordinating with Fagin, intercepts Oliver on the street and—with Sikes's physical force—drags him back into the criminal gang by falsely claiming him as her runaway brother before horrified bystanders.

Sikes and Nancy drag Oliver back to Fagin's den, where the gang mocks him, strips his gentleman's clothes, and Nancy violently defends Oliver against Fagin's beating before fainting, after which Oliver is locked in the dark.

Mr. Bumble travels to London on parish business, spots Mr. Brownlow's reward advertisement for Oliver, visits him and delivers a damning false account of Oliver's character, causing Brownlow to denounce the boy as an impostor.
Fagin uses threats, isolation, and the Dodger's persuasion to slowly wear down Oliver's resistance and groom him into accepting a life of crime.
Fagin visits Sikes and Nancy to plan the Chertsey burglary, and the three agree to use Oliver as the small boy needed to break in, with Nancy tasked to fetch him the next night.

Fagin warns Oliver to obey Bill Sikes without question, then Nancy delivers Oliver to Sikes, who loads a pistol and threatens to shoot him if he speaks, before leading him out on a criminal errand at dawn.

Sikes drags Oliver through pre-dawn London and Smithfield market, then by cart and foot across the countryside to a ruinous isolated house near Shepperton, where Oliver, terrified, suspects Sikes intends to murder him.
Sikes and Toby Crackit bring Oliver to Chertsey, force him through a small window to open a house for burglary, but are discovered, shots are fired, and Oliver is wounded as they flee.

Mr. Bumble visits workhouse matron Mrs. Corney, they share tea and flirt until he kisses her, whereupon they are interrupted by news that a dying pauper, Old Sally, insists on revealing a secret before she dies.
Dying workhouse inmate Old Sally confesses to matron Mrs. Corney that she stole a gold keepsake from Oliver's dying mother years ago, but expires before revealing what the object was.

Fagin and his gang idle in their den until Toby Crackit arrives haggard and alone, confessing the burglary failed, Oliver was shot and abandoned in a ditch, and Sikes is unaccounted for — sending Fagin fleeing the house in panic.

Fagin, agitated after the failed robbery, scours the criminal haunts of Saffron Hill seeking Monks, stops to check on a drunk and anguished Nancy at Sikes's lodgings, then holds a tense secret midnight meeting with Monks at his own den, where they argue over what to do with Oliver and are briefly terrified by the shadow of a figure on the wall.

Mr Bumble snoops through Mrs Corney's belongings, discovers her savings, proposes marriage and is accepted, then stops at the undertaker's to order a pauper coffin, before the narrator pivots to check on Oliver still lying wounded in a ditch.

After the failed burglary Sikes abandons wounded Oliver in a ditch and flees; Oliver regains consciousness, staggers back to the very house they tried to rob, collapses at the door, and is taken in — with the young lady (Rose Maylie) urging the servants to treat him kindly.

Doctor Losberne arrives at the Maylie household, examines the wounded intruder shot by Giles, discovers the "thief" is merely a boy (Oliver), and urges Mrs. Maylie and Rose to see the patient before any further action is taken.

Rose Maylie and Mrs. Maylie visit the wounded, sleeping Oliver and are struck by his innocence; the doctor manoeuvres to shield him from arrest by pressuring Giles and Brittles to doubt their identification, while Oliver recounts his history to the ladies—until the unexpected arrival of Bow Street officers threatens the plan.

Bow Street officers Blathers and Duff investigate the Maylie burglary; Dr. Losberne cleverly misdirects them by presenting the feverish Oliver as accidentally wounded by a spring-gun, the servants' contradictory testimony and the harmless pistol charge undermine any case against Oliver, and he is ultimately bailed into Mrs. Maylie's and Losberne's custody.

Oliver recovers from his wounds under the Maylies' care, travels with Dr. Losberne to find Mr. Brownlow but learns he has emigrated to the West Indies, then spends three blissful months in a country cottage where peaceful rural life, education, and the affection of Rose and Mrs. Maylie transform him into a happy, domesticated member of their household.

Rose Maylie falls suddenly into a dangerous fever; Oliver rushes to send for a doctor and on the errand collides with a mysterious hostile stranger who collapses in a fit upon seeing him; after days hovering near death, Rose at last shows signs of recovery.

Harry Maylie arrives at the cottage, learns Rose is recovering, and privately declares his love for Rose to his mother (who warns of Rose's uncertain birth); meanwhile Oliver dozes at a window and wakes to find Fagin and Monks peering in at him.

Oliver spots Fagin and Monks lurking at the cottage window but the search finds no trace of them; Harry Maylie then declares his love to Rose, who refuses him—insisting the stain on her unknown origins would blight his prospects—though she admits she returns his feelings.

Harry Maylie departs with Dr. Losberne, privately enlisting Oliver to send him fortnightly letters about Rose and the household without telling the ladies, while Rose watches the carriage vanish and weeps in silence behind the curtain.

Mr. Bumble, stripped of his beadle status and henpecked by his new wife, is approached in a pub by the mysterious Monks, who bribes him for information about the woman who knew Oliver Twist's mother, arranging a secret meeting for the following night.

Mr and Mrs Bumble meet Monks at a derelict riverside building at night, sell him the locket and wedding ring stolen from Oliver's dead mother, and watch him destroy the evidence by dropping it through a trap-door into the river.

Nancy, nursing the ill and abusive Sikes, secretly eavesdrops on a private meeting between Fagin and Monks at Fagin's den, then drugs Sikes with laudanum and races across London to seek out Rose Maylie at her hotel.

Nancy secretly meets Rose Maylie and reveals that Monks has conspired with Fagin to corrupt Oliver and suppress proof of his true identity, then refuses rescue and agrees to meet Rose on London Bridge every Sunday night.

Rose Maylie, wrestling with keeping Nancy's secret, brings Oliver to Craven Street where he is joyfully reunited with Mr Brownlow, and the assembled group resolves to unmask Monks through private stratagem rather than legal prosecution in order to recover Oliver's stolen inheritance.

Noah Claypole and Charlotte arrive in London fleeing their stolen money, stumble into the Three Cripples tavern, where Fagin secretly observes them, then recruits Noah into his criminal gang under threat of exposure, assigning him to the "kinchin lay" — robbing small children of their errand money.

Fagin recruits Noah Claypole (Bolter) into his gang and sends him to spy on the Artful Dodger's court hearing, where the Dodger defies the magistrates with comic bravado before being committed for transportation.

Nancy fails her appointed midnight meeting with Rose Maylie because Sikes physically detains her past the hour, while Fagin, suspecting her of secret dealings, begins scheming to use blackmail and the threat of Sikes's violence to bring her under his full control.
Fagin recruits Noah Claypole as a spy to tail Nancy, suspecting she has contacted outsiders; after six nights' wait, on a Sunday he sends Noah to follow her as she slips out alone at night.

At midnight on London Bridge, Nancy secretly meets Mr Brownlow and Rose Maylie, gives them details to identify and trap Monks, refuses to betray Fagin or accept rescue for herself, and is covertly watched throughout by Noah Claypole, who immediately rushes to report to Fagin.
Fagin uses Noah Claypole's eyewitness account to inflame Bill Sikes with news of Nancy's secret meetings with gentlefolk, and Sikes rushes home and beats Nancy to death as she pleads for mercy.

After murdering Nancy, Bill Sikes flees London and wanders the countryside haunted by visions of her corpse, unable to escape his guilt, before resolving to return to London and seek refuge through Fagin.

Mr Brownlow forces Monks into a private confrontation, reveals knowledge of the destroyed will and Oliver's true parentage as Leeford's illegitimate son, and extracts a sworn promise of full confession and restitution, while news arrives that the murderer (Sikes) is about to be caught and Fagin seized.

Sikes, hunted by an enormous mob at Jacob's Island after Nancy's murder, attempts rope-escape from the rooftop but, hallucinating Nancy's eyes, loses his balance and accidentally hangs himself; his dog leaps after him and dies too, while Fagin is noted to have been captured the same day.

Mr Brownlow compels Monks to publicly confess Oliver's true parentage and the destroyed will; the Bumbles are disgraced over the stolen locket; Rose Maylie is revealed as Agnes Fleming's sister and therefore Oliver's aunt; and Harry Maylie proposes marriage to Rose, who accepts now that her illegitimate stigma is lifted — the chapter ends with the death of Dick.

Fagin is convicted and sentenced to hang; on his final night in Newgate, Mr Brownlow and Oliver visit him in the condemned cell, where Fagin—deranged with terror—reveals the location of Monks's hidden papers before being dragged away screaming by guards.

The final chapter dispenses the fates of all characters: Oliver is adopted by Mr Brownlow, Rose Maylie marries Harry, Monks squanders his inheritance and dies in prison, the Bumbles sink into workhouse poverty, and the novel closes on Agnes's nameless memorial tablet.

Testi/Dickens/Atomized/Our_Mutual_Friend.plot: Book 1 table of contents lists 17 chapter titles that trace the introduction of the Wilfer family, Boffin's Bower, Silas Wegg's self-interest, a marriage contract, "Podsnappery" satire, and the tracking and downfall of a bird of prey.

Unit is table of contents for Book 2 ("Birds of a Feather"), listing 16 chapter titles spanning educational encounters, romantic entanglements, an innocent elopement, an orphan making his will, a successor, and birds of prey — no narrative prose or named characters appear.

Book 3 ("A Long Lane") charts Nicodemus Boffin's progressive moral deterioration as he falls into bad company, while Silas Wegg and Mr Venus (the "Friendly Move") tighten their scheme to use documents found in the dust heaps to extort him, culminating in Wegg preparing his figurative grindstone for Boffin's nose.

Book 4 table of contents lists 17 episodes tracing Boffin's feigned miserliness, Bella and John Harmon's secret elopement, Bradley Headstone's near-fatal attack on Eugene Wrayburn and Lizzie's rescue, Jenny Wren's pivotal discovery, and the final checkmate of Silas Wegg's extortion scheme.
This unit is solely the section heading for Book One ("The Cup and the Lip"), containing no narrative action or characters.

Gaffer Hexam and daughter Lizzie dredge the Thames at night, hauling a drowned body in tow while Gaffer repudiates his former partner for robbing the living — a sin he considers far worse than plundering the dead.

At a glittering Veneering dinner party Mortimer narrates the life of John Harmon—son of a dust-contractor, exiled after pleading for his sister, recalled to inherit a vast fortune on condition he marry a specified girl—and the chapter ends when a note arrives mid-story announcing that Harmon has drowned.

Mortimer Lightwood and Eugene Wrayburn follow Gaffer Hexam's son to the riverside hovel, view the drowned body of John Harmon at the police station alongside a mysterious agitated stranger who signs himself "Julius Handford," while at home Lizzie Hexam confides to Charley her vision of his rise through education and her own self-sacrifice; the inquest returns an open verdict on the suspicious "Harmon Murder," which then drifts into public notoriety.

The impoverished Wilfer family is introduced, with Bella bitterly lamenting her fate as a "kind of widow" jilted by the Harmon will, while a mysterious, reserved lodger signs the lease under the name John Rokesmith—hinted at the chapter's close to be the same man as Julius Handford and, by extension, John Harmon himself in disguise.

Illiterate but newly wealthy Nicodemus Boffin hires one-legged street vendor Silas Wegg to read Gibbon's Decline and Fall aloud at Boffin's Bower, while Wegg privately schemes to exploit the arrangement for as much profit as possible.

Miss Abbey Potterson warns Lizzie Hexam that her father Gaffer is suspected of murder, urges her to leave him; Lizzie refuses, instead sends brother Charley away to school for a better future, then returns home to face Gaffer with news of Charley's departure while he is himself shunned by the riverside community.

Silas Wegg visits Mr Venus's dim bone-and-taxidermy shop, learns Venus still holds his amputated leg unsold and cannot fit it into any "miscellaneous" skeleton, hears Venus's melancholy complaint that his beloved rejects him because of his grisly profession, and picks up a rumour that hidden wealth may lie in the Harmon dust mounds before stumping away to the Bower.

Boffin formally inherits the Harmon fortune at Lightwood's office, instructs a £10,000 murder reward and a will leaving all to Mrs. Boffin, briefly meets Eugene Wrayburn, then is followed on Fleet Street by a mysterious stranger who names himself Rokesmith—Harmon in disguise—and proposes to serve as his secretary.

Newly rich Mr and Mrs Boffin plan fashionable life, consult Rev. Milvey about adopting an orphan to bear John Harmon's name, then visit the Wilfers to invite Bella into their household, where she notices lodger Mr Rokesmith react with uncanny alarm at mention of the dead Harmon boy.

Alfred Lammle and Sophronia Akershem marry at the Veneering house, but on their Isle of Wight honeymoon discover each deceived the other about having property, and they forge a cynical pact to collude as adventurers against the world.

At Podsnap's birthday dinner for his daughter Georgiana, Mr Podsnap performs English self-satisfaction for a foreign guest and silences talk of street starvation, while the Lammles cynically cultivate shy Georgiana's friendship, privately scheming to exploit her for money.

Roger Riderhood visits Lightwood's office and, lured by the reward money, accuses his former partner Gaffer Hexam of the Harmon murder, claiming Hexam confessed; Lightwood, Wrayburn, and the police inspector then move to apprehend Hexam at the Six Jolly Fellowships.

Eugene Wrayburn, Lightwood, and Mr Inspector spend a night staking out Gaffer Hexam's riverside dwelling—during which Eugene secretly watches a weeping, solitary Lizzie through her window—until Riderhood returns from the river to report Gaffer's boat found empty and adrift.

Gaffer Hexam's drowned corpse is hauled from the Thames, entangled in his own rope, and Mr Inspector methodically reconstructs how Gaffer fell overboard in a squall and accidentally strangled himself while trying to loot a floating body.

Boffin hires John Rokesmith (the disguised John Harmon) as his secretary, installs Wegg as caretaker of the Bower, then is alarmed when Mrs Boffin is visited by ghostly visions of the old miser's face and the dead children throughout the house.

John Harmon (as Secretary Rokesmith) settles into Boffin's affairs, avoids Lightwood, accompanies Mrs Boffin to Brentford to assess orphan Johnny at Betty Higden's home, then encounters Bella Wilfer in the fields and reveals his secretarial role while hinting at her prospects with the Boffins.

Boffins settle into their aristocratic mansion and are besieged by social climbers and beggars of every stripe seeking their fortune, Bella Wilfer moves in as their guest, while Wegg secretly prowls the old house probing dust-mounds in search of something hidden.
Unit is a bare section-title page marking the start of Book the Second ("Birds of a Feather") with no narrative content or characters present.

Bradley Headstone, the rigidly self-made schoolmaster, accompanies Charley Hexam to visit his sister Lizzie, where they encounter Eugene Wrayburn, igniting Bradley's jealous fixation on Lizzie and establishing the central rivalry between the two men.

Bradley Headstone accompanies pupil Charley Hexam to visit Lizzie at Jenny Wren's lodging, becomes visibly disturbed by Lizzie's presence, and on the return crossing spots Eugene Wrayburn loitering nearby — planting the seed of Headstone's jealous fixation on both.

Eugene Wrayburn visits Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren, persuades Lizzie to overcome her pride and accept his offer of funded education lessons; afterward Jenny's drunken father staggers home and she scolds him with stern maternal authority, enacting a stark parent-child role reversal.

Veneering buys a parliamentary seat at Pocket-Breaches by mobilizing his social network (Twemlow, Podsnap, Lady Tippins, Boots, Brewer) in a frantic day of performative "work," and is duly elected despite knowing none of his constituents.

The Lammles cultivate Georgiana Podsnap's friendship and then orchestrate a dinner and opera outing to engineer a match between her and the awkward Fledgeby, while privately revealing their scheme is driven by Georgiana's money.

Fledgeby breakfasts with Lammle, agreeing to pursue Georgiana Podsnap through their scheming compact, then visits his secret moneylending front (run by the Jewish elder Riah under the name Pubsey & Co.), where he finds Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren resting on the rooftop, and Jenny delivers her otherworldly vision of peace in imagined death.

Charley Hexam and Bradley Headstone confront Eugene Wrayburn at his chambers, demanding he cease his secret visits and tutoring of Lizzie Hexam; Eugene deflects with languid contempt while Bradley's anguished jealousy erupts, and Eugene afterwards admits to Mortimer he cannot explain his own intentions toward Lizzie.

Silas Wegg enlists Mr Venus into a secret "friendly move" — a pact to secretly search Boffin's dust mounds for hidden money or wills — before John Harmon (as Rokesmith) appears at the window to deliver a message, unsettling the conspirators.

Bella visits her irritable family, then escapes with her father for a joyful Greenwich dinner funded by a Boffin gift, confessing she intends to marry for money while wishing the late John Harmon had lived to marry her.

Rokesmith (secretly John Harmon) and Mrs Boffin, with Bella, transport the gravely ill orphan Johnny to a children's hospital after overcoming Betty Higden's terror of institutional charity; the doctor privately declares it too late, and Johnny dies peacefully bequeathing his toys and asking for a kiss for "the boofer lady."

After the death of young Johnny, the Boffins resolve not to revive the name "John Harmon" and, prompted by Mrs Boffin's desire for unselfish charity, choose ungainly Sloppy — who insists on still caring for Betty Higden — as their new ward.

Bradley Headstone visits Jenny Wren's home to confront Lizzie Hexam and demand she reject Eugene Wrayburn's help in favor of her brother's plans, but Lizzie refuses him calmly, and afterward she secretly confesses her love for Wrayburn to Jenny through a fantasy of a wealthy lady.

John Harmon, disguised as a sailor carrying George Radfoot's knife and coat, confronts Rogue Riderhood at his Limehouse pawnshop, exposes his false testimony against Gaffer Hexam, and compels him to agree to sign a written retraction to clear the Hexam family name.

John Harmon, living as secretary John Rokesmith, wanders Limehouse reliving the night he was drugged and nearly drowned, resolves in an extended interior monologue to keep his true identity buried forever, then returns to the Boffin house where Bella Wilfer angrily rejects his declaration of love.

Rokesmith (the disguised John Harmon) resolves to keep his buried identity, dispatches Riderhood's exonerating recantation to Lizzie Hexam by post, hires Bradley Headstone as tutor for Sloppy—uncovering Headstone's fierce jealousy of Eugene Wrayburn—and bids farewell to the proudly independent Betty Higden as she departs to earn her own keep on the road.

Bradley Headstone makes a desperate marriage proposal to Lizzie Hexam in a churchyard; she firmly refuses him, her brother Charley furiously disowns her for it, and as she weeps alone an elderly Riah comforts her before Eugene Wrayburn appears, exposing himself as Headstone's unnamed rival and the true reason behind Lizzie's rejection.

At the Lammles' hollow first-anniversary breakfast, Mortimer Lightwood reveals that Lizzie Hexam has mysteriously vanished, while Mrs Lammle secretly confesses to Twemlow that she and her husband are conspiring to marry Georgiana to Fledgeby for money, imploring him to warn the girl's father.
This unit contains only the title heading "BOOK THE THIRD — A LONG LANE" with no narrative content.

Fledgeby reviews accounts with Riah (whom he uses as a front for his moneylending), receives Lammle's news that the Podsnap scheme has collapsed, then interrogates Riah until he learns that Riah helped Lizzie Hexam flee to safety and that her dangerous pursuer is Wrayburn.

Jenny Wren and Riah visit Miss Abbey Potterson at the Six Jolly Fellowship Porters to present a document vindicating Lizzie Hexam's father, and the visit ends when a foggy river collision brings in a recovered body revealed to be Riderhood.

Rogue Riderhood is dragged from the river after being struck by a steamer and brought to Miss Abbey's pub, where bystanders labor to revive him; hope briefly flickers that near-death will reform him, but he regains consciousness as sullen and irredeemable as before.

Bella joins her family for the Wilfer wedding anniversary, plays cook amid Mrs Wilfer's martyrdom, then confides to her father four secrets: Rokesmith (John Harmon) proposed and was refused, Lightwood would propose, the Boffins plan to portion her on marriage, and Mr Boffin is visibly being corrupted and hardened by his new prosperity.

Bella watches Boffin grow miserly and tyrannical toward his secretary (Rokesmith/Harmon) — humiliating him over wages, obsessively hoarding books about misers, and preaching money-worship — while Mrs Lammle cultivates a treacherous friendship with Bella and coaxes out the secret of Rokesmith's declaration.

Wegg and Venus conspire at the Bower while Boffin arrives with miser biographies for Wegg to read aloud; afterward Boffin secretly digs up a bottle buried atop the mound, Wegg and Venus spy on him, and Wegg—maddened by greed—tries to seize Boffin by force but is wrestled down by Venus as Boffin escapes.

Wegg reveals to Venus that he found a hidden cash-box containing John Harmon's earlier will (which largely benefits the Crown over Boffin), and the two conspirators argue over custody of the document before agreeing to lie in wait and eventually extort Boffin for half his fortune, with Venus taking physical possession of the will as leverage over both Boffin and his own partner.

Old Betty Higden, dying after a long flight from parish charity, collapses near a mill where Lizzie Hexam finds her, receives the letter for the Boffins, and promises never to surrender Betty to the parish — Betty dies in her arms.

At Betty Higden's riverside burial, Bella Wilfer and John Harmon (disguised as Secretary Rokesmith) travel to the paper-mill village where Lizzie Hexam is hiding; Bella and Lizzie form an intimate friendship, and Lizzie reveals she fled a violent suitor (Headstone) while carrying a secret, selfless love for a gentleman far above her station (Wrayburn).

Eugene Wrayburn visits Jenny Wren, then uses her drunken father Mr Dolls as a paid informant to locate Lizzie Hexam, before leading Bradley Headstone—who has been shadowing him—on an exhausting nocturnal chase across London.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Alls_Well_that_E.plot: The King of France discusses the Florentine-Sienese war with his lords, then warmly receives young Bertram at Paris, eulogizing his late father's honor and lamenting his own declining health.

Bertram woos Diana with false vows and surrenders his ancestral ring in exchange for a midnight assignation; Diana, already party to Helen's bed-trick scheme, agrees while privately vowing to cozen him without yielding her chastity.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Antony_and_Cleop.plot: Cleopatra, terrified of Antony's fury, flees to her monument and sends Mardian to falsely tell Antony she has killed herself.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/As_You_Like_It/A.plot: Duke Frederick threatens Oliver: find Orlando within a year or lose lands and be banished; Oliver admits he never loved his brother, which only enrages Frederick further.

Rosalind (disguised as Ganymede) interrupts Phoebe's cruel rejection of Silvius, rebukes Phoebe's pride, but inadvertently causes Phoebe to fall in love with "Ganymede," after which Phoebe resolves to send Silvius with a taunting letter to the disguised Rosalind.

Rosalind (disguised as Ganymede) exchanges barbs with Jaques on melancholy, then conducts a playful mock-wooing and mock-marriage ceremony with Orlando, warning him of love's transience before he departs to attend the Duke.

Oliver arrives in the forest to deliver Orlando's bloodied napkin to Rosalind and Celia, recounting how Orlando saved him from a snake and lioness, whereupon Rosalind faints at the news, nearly exposing her female identity beneath the Ganymede disguise.

Rosalind (as Ganymede) promises Orlando, Oliver, Phoebe, and Silvius that all shall be married tomorrow, orchestrating a fourfold resolution while Oliver announces he will wed Aliena and surrender his inheritance to Orlando.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Coriolanus/Act_1.plot: Defeated Aufidius, bloody after the fall of Corioli, vows to kill Coriolanus by any means — fair fight, treachery, or ambush — abandoning all scruple of honour or hospitality.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Coriolanus/Act_4.plot: Coriolanus bids farewell to his mother Volumnia, wife Virgilia, and friends Menenius and Cominius before departing into exile, urging them to suppress tears and promising to remain true to himself.

After Coriolanus's banishment, Volumnia and Virgilia confront the tribunes Sicinius and Brutus in the street, unleashing furious curses and reproaches before the tribunes retreat and the grieving women depart with Menenius.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Coriolanus/Act_5.plot: After Cominius reports that Coriolanus coldly refused to hear him or acknowledge his name, the tribunes persuade a reluctant Menenius to attempt his own appeal, while Cominius doubts it will succeed and pins last hope on Volumnia and Virgilia.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Cymbeline/Act_2/.plot: Posthumus rages in misogynistic soliloquy blaming Innogen and all women for vice after believing her unfaithful; then Cymbeline, the Queen, and Cloten jointly defy Rome's ambassador Lucius and refuse to pay Caesar's tribute, inviting war.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Cymbeline/Act_3/.plot: Belarius leads his adopted sons Guiderius and Arviragus from their cave for the hunt, praises wilderness over corrupt court life while they chafe at their ignorance of the world, then reveals in soliloquy that he kidnapped them as Cymbeline's heirs in revenge for his own unjust banishment.

Exhausted and starving, Innogen in male disguise stumbles into Belarius and his foster-sons' cave, is discovered taking food, and is welcomed as a companion named Fidele, unwittingly meeting her own lost brothers.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Cymbeline/Act_4/.plot: Cloten, wearing Posthumus' stolen garments, delivers a boastful soliloquy declaring himself Posthumus' superior in every way and vowing to kill Posthumus, rape Innogen, and return her to Cymbeline.
Belarius urges retreat to the mountains to avoid Roman forces, but Guiderius and Arviragus insist on joining the battle, shaming idleness in hiding; Belarius yields and all three march to fight.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Hamlet/Act_1/Sce.plot: Laertes warns Ophelia not to trust Hamlet's love before departing; Polonius then interrogates Ophelia about Hamlet's courtship and commands her to refuse all further contact with him.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Hamlet/Act_3/Sce.plot: Claudius and Polonius spy on Hamlet's encounter with Ophelia during which Hamlet delivers the "To be or not to be" soliloquy and then cruelly rejects Ophelia, sending her to a nunnery; Claudius concludes Hamlet's behavior is not love-madness and resolves to send him to England.

Claudius dispatches Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to escort Hamlet to England, then kneels alone in failed prayer over his brother's murder; Hamlet finds him praying but sheathes his sword, resolving to kill him in a damned state rather than send his soul to heaven.

Hamlet confronts Gertrude in her chamber, kills Polonius hiding behind the arras, forces Gertrude to face her moral corruption, and receives the Ghost's reminder to stay on course, before dragging Polonius's body away.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Hamlet/Act_4/Sce.plot: Gertrude reports to Claudius that Hamlet in a mad fit has killed Polonius; Claudius sends Rosencrantz and Guildenstern to find Hamlet and retrieve the body, and resolves to ship Hamlet out of Denmark.
Hamlet, having hidden Polonius's body, mocks Rosencrantz and Guildenstern as royal sponges and refuses to reveal the body's location before running off with them in pursuit.
Claudius interrogates Hamlet about Polonius's body, then dispatches him to England with secret orders for his execution.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Henry_V/Act_2/Sc.plot: Chorus narrates England's war fever as Henry readies to sail for France, then exposes a French-funded conspiracy by Cambridge, Scrope, and Grey to kill the king at Southampton before he can embark.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Henry_V/Act_3/Sc.plot: Henry V delivers his famous "Once more unto the breach" speech, urging his troops to charge Harfleur's walls with fierce resolve and pride in their English heritage.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Henry_V/Act_4/Sc.plot: Chorus describes the tense eve of Agincourt — overconfident French gambling while the weary English wait in dread — then celebrates Henry V's nocturnal walkabout among his troops as a source of morale and comfort.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Henry_V/Act_5/Sc.plot: Chorus bridges narrative gap: describes Henry V's humble return from France to jubilant London crowds, his refusal to parade war trophies, then skips ahead past diplomatic negotiations to Harry's return to France.
Fluellen beats Pistol and forces him to eat the leek as payback for mocking Welsh customs; Pistol then learns his wife Nell is dead and vows to return to England as a petty thief.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Julius_Caesar/Ac.plot: Brutus orders Messala to ride and signal his legions to attack at once, sensing weakness in Octavius's wing.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Macbeth/Act_1/Sc.plot: Duncan praises Macbeth and Banquo, names Malcolm Prince of Cumberland, and plans to visit Macbeth's castle; in an aside Macbeth reveals his dark ambition to overcome Malcolm as an obstacle.

Macbeth soliloquizes doubts about killing Duncan, then Lady Macbeth enters and overrides his hesitation through taunts and a detailed drugging-the-chamberlains plan, ending with Macbeth resolved to proceed.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Macbeth/Act_2/Sc.plot: Macbeth returns to Lady Macbeth immediately after killing Duncan; he is paralysed by guilt and unable to return the daggers, so Lady Macbeth does it herself, while Macbeth fears his bloodied hands can never be washed clean.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Macbeth/Act_5/Sc.plot: Macduff enters the battlefield seeking Macbeth alone, driven by guilt over his family's deaths, and refuses to fight lesser soldiers.
Macbeth and Macduff fight; Macduff reveals he was born by caesarean section, shattering Macbeth's belief in his charmed life, yet Macbeth refuses to yield and is slain.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Measure_for_Meas.plot: Angelo and Escalus prepare for the Duke's return to the city, then Angelo alone confesses in soliloquy that he has deflowered (as he believes) Isabella and still had Claudio executed, and fears the consequences of his corruption.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Much_Ado_About_N.plot: Antonio reports to Leonato that a servant overheard Don Pedro confess love for Hero to Claudio and plan to declare it at the night's dance, so Leonato resolves to warn Hero to prepare her answer.

Don Pedro, Claudio, and Leonato mock Benedick's obvious lovesick change, while Don John arrives to plant doubt in Claudio and Don Pedro about Hero's fidelity, inviting them to spy on her chamber window the night before the wedding.
Claudio and Don Pedro, dressed in black, visit Leonato's monument at night, where Claudio reads an epitaph and sings a solemn hymn for Hero before departing at dawn to attend the planned wedding.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Othello/Act_3/Sc.plot: Othello hands Iago letters to deliver to the pilot for the senate, then leads gentlemen to inspect the fortifications.

Iago plants seeds of jealousy in Othello's mind about Desdemona and Cassio, fabricates dream-evidence and the handkerchief as proof of adultery, and secures Othello's vow of revenge — ending with Othello ordering Cassio's death and promoting Iago to lieutenant.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Othello/Act_4/Sc.plot: Othello publicly humiliates Desdemona by calling her a whore while Emilia and Iago witness her distress; Iago then manipulates the duped Roderigo into agreeing to murder Cassio so that Othello cannot leave Cyprus.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Pericles/Scenes/.plot: Gower narrates how Pericles receives news that Antiochus is dead and Tyre demands his return as king; he departs from Simonides' court with the pregnant Thaisa, and a violent storm at sea sends Thaisa into labor.
Pericles, departing Tarsus after his wife Thaisa's death at sea, entrusts his newborn daughter Marina to Cleon and Dionyza's care, vowing not to cut his hair until she is married.
Dionyza defends Marina's murder to a horrified Cleon, rationalizing it as done for their own daughter's benefit, and plans to deceive Pericles with a false monument and fabricated grief.

Gower narrates Pericles sailing to Tarsus to reclaim Marina; Cleon and Dionyza show him a tomb (dumb show), deceiving him into believing Marina dead, whereupon he departs in sackcloth and overwhelming grief while Gower reads Marina's false epitaph.

Gower narrates that Marina has escaped the brothel and thrives in an honest house through her arts of singing, dancing, and needlework, while Pericles' ship arrives at the very city where she dwells, setting the stage for their reunion.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Richard_Duke_of_.plot: After victory at Barnet, Edward IV and brothers Clarence and Richard learn Queen Margaret has landed from France with forces marching toward Tewkesbury, and Edward orders immediate pursuit.

Richard of Gloucester visits the imprisoned King Henry VI in the Tower, murders him twice with his dagger, then delivers a cold soliloquy proclaiming his plan to eliminate Clarence and all rivals until he alone holds power.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Richard_II/Act_1.plot: Duchess of Gloucester urges John of Gaunt to avenge her husband's murder, but Gaunt refuses, arguing that since Richard II — God's anointed deputy — ordered the killing, only heaven can exact revenge.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Romeo_and_Juliet.plot: Capulet tells Paris to woo Juliet at his feast; Romeo and Benvolio chance upon the servant's invitation list and decide to attend, Romeo hoping to see Rosaline.
Lady Capulet and the Nurse summon Juliet and urge her to consider marrying the suitor Paris, who will attend the Capulet feast that night.

themes: transition from old to new desire
Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Romeo_and_Juliet.plot: The Chorus declares Romeo's old infatuation dead, replaced by mutual love with Juliet, and notes that though they are enemies barred from easy meeting, passion lends them the power and means to find each other.
Romeo secretly enters the Capulet orchard at night, overhears Juliet lamenting the barrier of his name, they declare mutual love, and Juliet proposes to arrange their marriage the following day.
Romeo visits Friar Laurence at dawn, declares his new love for Juliet and begs him to marry them that day; the Friar agrees, hoping the match will end the Capulet-Montague feud.
Juliet impatiently awaits the Nurse's return with Romeo's message; after prolonged teasing and complaint, the Nurse reveals Romeo waits at Friar Laurence's cell to make Juliet his wife.
Friar Laurence cautions Romeo against violent passion, Juliet arrives and the lovers exchange brief words of joy, then Friar leads them away to be married by the Church.

Juliet eagerly awaits Romeo's arrival, but the Nurse brings news of Tybalt's death at Romeo's hand and Romeo's banishment, plunging Juliet from joyful anticipation into anguish; torn between grief for her cousin and loyalty to her husband, she sends her ring to Romeo for a final farewell.

Romeo learns from Friar Laurence that the Prince has sentenced him to banishment rather than death; he collapses in despair, attempts self-stabbing, but is rebuked by the Friar and comforted by the Nurse bearing Juliet's ring, then is urged to spend the night with Juliet before fleeing to Mantua.
Capulet, citing Tybalt's recent death, abruptly decides to wed Juliet to Paris on Thursday and instructs his wife to inform her.

Romeo and Juliet part at dawn after their wedding night; Juliet is then told she must marry Paris on Thursday, her father Capulet rages violently when she refuses, her mother abandons her, and the Nurse betrays her by advising she comply — leaving Juliet alone, resolved to seek Friar Laurence's help or die.
Friar Laurence gives Juliet a sleeping potion to fake her death and avoid forced marriage to Paris, promising to alert Romeo so he can retrieve her from the Capulet tomb.

Juliet dismisses the Nurse and Lady Capulet, then alone delivers a fearful soliloquy weighing every danger of the potion—poison, premature waking in the tomb, Tybalt's ghost—before steeling herself and drinking it, collapsing onto her bed.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/The_Comedy_of_Er.plot: Antipholus of Syracuse arrives in Ephesus, dispatches Dromio of Syracuse to the inn with gold, then is accosted by Dromio of Ephesus — his twin's servant — who knows nothing of the money but demands he come home to dinner; confusing the two Dromios, Antipholus beats him, then suspects theft and fears the city is full of sorcerers and cheats.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/The_History_of_K.plot: Edmund forges a letter to frame Edgar as plotting against Gloucester, tricks their father into suspecting Edgar of parricide ambition, then manipulates Edgar into hiding — securing his own rise through calculated villainy.

Gloucester confides to Edmund his plan to secretly aid the banished King Lear despite Cornwall's prohibition, then Edmund immediately resolves to betray his father to the Duke to gain his inheritance.

Kent, disguised, tells a gentleman how Cordelia wept on reading letters about Lear's plight, explains that Lear's burning shame over his cruelty to her keeps him from reunion, and warns that Albany and Cornwall's armies are already moving.
After French forces are defeated and Lear and Cordelia are captured, Edgar urges the despairing blind Gloucester to flee with him, counseling that men must endure their fate — "ripeness is all."

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/The_Tragedy_of_K.plot: Kent, disguised, meets a gentleman on the stormy heath: reveals Lear rages alone with the Fool, warns of Albany-Cornwall rift and French spies, and dispatches the gentleman to find Cordelia bearing a ring as proof of his identity.
After Lear and Cordelia's forces are defeated and taken prisoner, Edgar leads the blind Gloucester away from the field, urging him to endure with the maxim "ripeness is all."

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/The_Two_Gentleme.plot: Valentine departs for Milan while Proteus stays behind for love of Julia; Speed arrives and reveals Proteus's love letter to Julia got a cold reception, leaving Proteus resolved to send a better messenger.

Valentine, oblivious to his own lovesickness, writes a letter at Silvia's bidding to her "nameless friend," only to have Speed reveal that Silvia engineered the trick so Valentine unknowingly wrote a love letter to himself.

Proteus, alone, resolves to betray both Julia and Valentine — planning to inform Silvia's father of Valentine's secret elopement scheme so Valentine is banished and Proteus can pursue Silvia for himself.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/The_Two_Noble_Ki.plot: The three Queens process severally with their lords' hearses, sing a funeral dirge, exchange brief valedictions, and part — closing Act 1 on an image of death as the universal marketplace.

Palamon bursts from the bush still shackled, accuses Arcite of treachery for courting Emilia; Arcite denies dishonor and promises to secretly return with food, filed shackles, and weapons so they can fight a fair duel for Emilia's love.

Arcite secretly brings imprisoned Palamon food, wine, and files in the forest; they drink and reminisce warmly until Palamon accuses Arcite of sighing for Emilia, their fragile truce collapses into insults, and Arcite promises to return with sword and armour so they can duel properly.

Palamon and his knights kneel before Venus's altar; Palamon delivers an elaborate prayer proclaiming his lifelong fidelity to love and begging the goddess for victory in the coming combat, then receives a favorable omen of music and fluttering doves.

Emilia prays alone at Diana's altar to remain a virgin or have the worthier suitor win, then receives ambiguous divine signs — a rose blooms and falls — suggesting she will be taken as a bride against her will.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/The_Winters_Tale.plot: Time as Chorus bridges a 16-year gap, noting Leontes remains shut up in grief while pivoting the action to Bohemia where Florizel and the now-grown Perdita will become the story's new focus.

Polixenes convinces Camillo to abandon plans to return to Sicilia and instead accompany him in disguise to a shepherd's cottage, where Florizel has been secretly spending time with a remarkable shepherd's daughter.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Timon_of_Athens/.plot: Despite having no money left, Timon orders Flavius to invite Lucius, Lucullus, and Sempronius to yet another feast, ignoring his steward's warnings about empty coffers.
Timon stands outside Athens walls, delivers furious curse calling for total societal breakdown, tears off clothes, and departs alone into the woods vowing hatred for all mankind.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Troilus_and_Cres.plot: Pandarus tells Cressida she must leave Troy and be exchanged for Antenor; Cressida refuses, swearing undying love for Troilus and vowing never to depart.
Troilus prepares to hand Cressida over to the Greeks for the prisoner exchange, likening himself to a priest sacrificing his own heart at an altar.
Achilles commands his Myrmidons to hold back their own blows and encircle Hector with weapons when found, declaring Hector's death decreed.
Hector, having just disarmed after battle, is surrounded by Achilles and his Myrmidons and murdered while defenseless; Achilles then orders the body dragged behind his horse.

Testi/Shakespeare/Plays/Twelfth_Night/Ac.plot: Orsino dispatches Viola (disguised as Cesario, having already won the Duke's trust in three days) to court Olivia on his behalf, while Viola privately reveals in an aside that she herself loves Orsino.
Sebastian parts from Antonio, reveals his twin sister drowned in the shipwreck and that he is bound for Orsino's court, while Antonio resolves to follow despite having enemies there.

Malvolio returns a ring to Viola (as Cesario) claiming Olivia sent it back, and Viola's soliloquy reveals she has no ring to return — deducing Olivia has fallen for her disguise, creating a hopeless love triangle.

Sebastian and Antonio arrive in Illyria; Antonio, fearing arrest for past offenses against the Count, gives Sebastian his purse and directs him to sightsee while he secures lodging at the Elephant inn.
Sebastian, bewildered by Olivia's gifts and unsure if he or she is mad, agrees to a secret betrothal ceremony with Olivia before a priest in a nearby chapel.

Testi/Chesterton/Atomized/alarms_and_dis.plot: A priest of a simple island republic builds a three-walled tower of lilies, crystal, and pure water crowned by a diamond, striving to create something worthy of the Sun-god.

After pirates invade and are finally repelled, an aged priest renounces classical perfectionism and inspires construction of a Gothic cathedral covered in ugly animals, declaring all creatures—however grotesque—praise God by pointing toward heaven.

Chesterton frames miscellaneous essays as medieval gargoyles on an invisible cathedral, ranging from a Cockney discovering rural England to a Faust puppet-play, a poor man crushed by a landlord yet parroting newspaper ideology, and the prehistoric White Horse vale, closing with King Alfred's last stand at Athelney as archetypal hero defending his island.

Testi/Chesterton/Atomized/AllThingsConsi.plot: Chesterton defends his collection of rushed journalistic essays, using them as a springboard to critique modernism as intellectual snobbery, philanthropic teetotalism as religious persecution, and anonymous corporate power as cowardly tyranny.

Chesterton defends his Cockney identity against a Yorkshire critic's slight, then argues that vulgar jokes — about bodily mishap, foreigners, bad cheese, mothers-in-law, and henpecked husbands — encode deep theological and social truths, and that popular comic papers are better prophets of democratic reality than intellectual sociologists.

Chesterton demolishes the genre of success-advice books, arguing they contain no real guidance, worship wealth as mysticism, and corrupt readers with avarice and snobbery rather than virtue, illustrating the point with the myth of Midas as a figure of failure misrepresented as triumph.

Chesterton argues that inconveniences like London floods or chasing one's hat are only unpleasant when viewed without imagination, and that a cheerful, poetic reframing turns every annoyance into adventure.

Chesterton dissects canvassing rules, defends direct political contact as honest versus silent corruption, then argues constitutional anomalies corrupt the mind by normalizing unreason, and that optimists — not pessimists — are the true reformers because injustice shocks them.

Chesterton argues that self-congratulation on lacking a vice is worthless when the absence stems from incapacity rather than virtue, using English political caricature's gentleness compared to Rowlandson and Gilray's brutality as proof that modern mildness reflects the unreality and class homogeneity of contemporary politics, not superior magnanimity.

Chesterton argues that English sporting defeats by Frenchmen and Belgians expose the hollowness of Anglo-Saxon superiority myths, contending that true national strength lies in broad average athleticism among common people rather than in exceptional individual champions.

Chesterton contrasts Paris and London through street names, statues, and city layout to argue that cities speak in signs, and that true education means learning to read those signs with fresh, unconditioned eyes.

Chesterton argues that true internationalism requires genuine national character, using French and English cultural differences as examples to show that superficial admiration of another nation's traits leads to misunderstanding and corruption of one's own identity.

Chesterton contrasts France's live debate over admitting Zola to the Panthéon with England's settled veneration of Shakespeare, then argues that Zola's deeper offense is not his obscenity but his bleak, joyless moral vision—making him worse than a pornographer because he is a pessimist who turned life itself into something loathsome.

Chesterton dissects the Outlook critic's defense of Oxford and Cambridge as cross-class institutions, demonstrating through irony and logical scrutiny that the universities remain plutocratic playgrounds for the governing class rather than engines of genuine social mixing.

Chesterton rebuts a correspondent who advocates communal kitchens as liberation for women, arguing instead that domestic work grants women genuine creative autonomy and authority, while dismissing "higher culture" as a vapid upper-class conceit worse than domestic drudgery.

Chesterton argues that modern "martyrdom" — Suffragettes chaining themselves to railings, Passive Resisters having teapots seized — fails as demonstration because it proves only sincerity, not transcendent strength, whereas true ancient martyrdom impressed pagans by showing believers draw joy from some superhuman source even amid extreme physical agony.

Chesterton classifies three legitimate forms of human secrecy, then argues that concealment of political party funds and purchase of peerages fits none of them, concluding England is ruled by an occult governing class that hides power because it cannot bear exposure.

Chesterton responds to a rebuke from the Scottish Patriotic Association for calling Edward VII "King of England," using the occasion to argue that genuine recognition of national sentiment—not mere political union—explains Britain's success with Scotland and failure with Ireland, then playfully proposes the king be named after every local town he visits.

Chesterton uses the Köpenick fraud — a man who impersonated a captain and bullied a mayor by pointing to bayonets as his "authority" — to argue that real soldiers never worship naked force, then pivots to show England has its own parallel weakness: deference to aristocratic manner substitutes for law, religion, and army alike.

Chesterton uses a newspaper report of English schoolboy Allen painting a Swiss general's statue red to argue that modern journalism and English public schools evade plain moral language, substituting euphemisms like "senseless" or "dastardly" for the simple verdict of right and wrong.

Chesterton critiques Dr. Horton's attack on the Yellow Press and Limerick craze, arguing that reformers conflate moral corruption with vulgarity, then proposes concrete remedies: jail editors who publish false news, suppress obscene court reporting, and mandate signed articles.

Chesterton argues that anonymous journalism enables hidden vested interests, demands proprietors' names be printed on all papers, and warns that modern editors suppressing public voices represent a broader drift away from democracy toward future tyranny.

Chesterton argues that modern newspaper reporters corrupt political speeches by cherry-picking vivid or concrete phrases while omitting the logical chain of argument, using Mark Antony's funeral oration and a Bernard Shaw speech as examples, and concludes that journalism's contempt for its audience ultimately produces obscurity rather than clarity.

Chesterton argues that modern journalism flatters the wealthy through subtle, credible-sounding praise — attributing depth to their trivial habits, calling their lives "simple" and "modest" — a more insidious deception than the old extravagant royal flattery, culminating in absurd eulogies even at their funerals.

Chesterton dissects a progressive theology pamphlet arguing science disproved the Fall and original sin, exposing the logical non-sequitur that physical science cannot speak to moral or spiritual realities, and concluding that religion was never genuinely shaken by materialism since honest atheism was always available from the start.

Chesterton recounts a newspaper anecdote of a soldier who listed his religion as "Methuselahite" (to live as long as possible), then uses this coinage to satirise modern philosophies that worship mere natural life, arguing such self-preservation is a form of cowardice and that the paradox of courage — one must risk life to keep it — dooms any religion of longevity to absurdity, as proven by the soldier's own act of enlisting.

Chesterton defends using grotesque/comic examples in serious argument, then rebukes a correspondent who criticizes his treatment of Spiritualism, concluding that spiritual contact requires prior faith and cannot be approached empirically.

Chesterton argues, using the hung Thaw trial jury as springboard, that demanded impartiality is really indifference or stupidity, and that the same fallacy infects religious debate—where reaching a conclusion brands a thinker a fanatic while withholding judgment is falsely praised as fairness.

Chesterton argues against phonetic spelling reform by showing that conventional spellings preserve the hidden etymological meaning of words (talent, republic, encourage, holiday, polite/police), and that stripping words to mere sound would accelerate the modern tendency to use language as dead counters rather than living coins.

Chesterton argues that European strength and humanitarianism share same root — imagination — and that adopting barbaric methods against "savages" would destroy Western moral authority, then extends critique to materialist thinking (scientific determinism, temperance reform, peace movements) as symptoms of a slide back toward barbarism.

Chesterton argues against the medicalized framing of "alcohol," contending that drink is dangerous not because it is bestial but because it can enslave, and proposes that open, socially integrated taverns with neighbourhood oversight would curb drunkenness better than prohibition.

Chesterton argues that the modern age is not one of demagogues but of mystagogues — people who gain status by being deliberately obscure and unintelligible — contrasting Gladstone with Disraeli, Michelangelo with Whistler, and skewering Lady Grove's book on social etiquette as a prime example of aristocratic mystification used to intimidate and exclude ordinary people.

Chesterton muses on a real newspaper named after Dickens's fictional corrupt rag, then dissects the absurd rivalry between Sudbury and Ipswich, each town proudly claiming to be the original Eatanswill, while arguing that Dickens's satire targeted all English elections, not any one place.

Chesterton argues against the view that fairy tales are immoral, contending instead that their core principle — happiness depends on obeying one absolute veto — makes them the deepest form of ethical teaching, rooting all moral law in wonder rather than rationalism.

Chesterton defends Fielding's Tom Jones against Victorian-era charges of immorality, arguing that the old moral tradition depicted vice to affirm an objective moral law standing apart from human behaviour, whereas modern writing falsely equates morality with depicting only virtuous characters.

Chesterton argues that Voltaire's crude mockery of Joan of Arc is more honest than Anatole France's (and Renan's) rationalist method of explaining saints by inventing unprovable psychological backstories, concluding Joan's mystical idealism was saner and more effective than modern secular pragmatism.

Chesterton eulogizes Francis Thompson as greatest English poet since Browning, praises his dual mastery of vast and minute imagery, then argues poets naturally gravitate toward Catholic religious symbolism because its simplicity is more poetically fertile than elaborate worldly ritual.

Chesterton argues that Christmas must be observed fully and ceremonially or not at all, defends meat-eating at Christmas against vegetarian critics by grounding it in human fellowship, and links this defence to his opposition to vivisection—both abuses arise when speculative sympathy for animals overrides concrete loyalty to mankind.

Testi/Chesterton/Atomized/All_I_Survey/C.plot: Chesterton dissects a philanthropist's remark that the rich should care for poor children "as if they were their own," arguing this slogan destroys parental autonomy, annihilates democracy, and amounts to state-sanctioned kidnapping dressed as idealism.

Chesterton attacks critics who demand deference to established authorities (Swinnerton on Stevenson) instead of direct engagement with the primary work, then defends Stevenson's tragic depth and sharpness of focus against the dismissal of him as merely "pretty."

Chesterton mocks a newspaper editorial condemning a turnpike as a "relic of medievalism," showing that printing, Parliament, and universities are equally medieval, that tolls fairly charge road-users rather than the local poor, and that the cult of ever-faster motor traffic risks mass slaughter.

Chesterton riffs on colossal American sculpture (Mount Rushmore) to fantasise about earth-scale art visible only from aircraft, then turns this into a parable: modern economic and political systems have grown so vast that no individual can oversee or control them.

Chesterton visits the Scottish War Memorial in Edinburgh Castle, contrasts its richly particular Gothic craftsmanship with the cold impersonality of the London Cenotaph, and argues — via a sculptor's Unicorn whose horn is bent into the design — that traditional local art is more vital and creative than abstract universalism.

Chesterton dismantles the cliché that Old Men caused WWI by exposing three hidden assumptions behind it, compares it to earlier feminist blame-the-males rhetoric, then warns that the Young Men now in power face an imminent new war on the Polish border no better equipped than their despised predecessors.

Chesterton argues that despite stark differences, French Catholic playwright Claudel and American Puritan poet Vachel Lindsay both unconsciously draw on the pervasive spirit of Spanish civilization, whose ornate, exuberant vitality underlies Western American culture and shapes both men's art.

Chesterton argues that revolutionary reputations (Byron, Swinburne) inevitably suffer later ridicule and dethronement while conservative figures (Burke, Morris, Newman) outlast them precisely because rebels were once overrated as prophets of the future.

Chesterton uses a woman's selective refusal of her husband's dress allowance as springboard to argue that modern society applies the ideal of independence arbitrarily—granted to women only in the domestic sphere while ignored everywhere else—exposing a chaotic, unprincipled approach to social reform and progress.

Chesterton uses a reductio-ad-absurdum about red-haired men to show how universal social theories distort historical truth, then contrasts Wells's progressive view of history with Spengler's closed-cycles model to demonstrate that such grand theories contradict each other and survive only by ignoring inconvenient facts.

Chesterton argues that eccentric literary styles — from Victorian portmanteau wordplay (Carroll) to modernist experiments (Joyce, Stein, Meredith) — inevitably fade rather than redirect tradition, and that literature always reverts to classical norms, making solemnity about novelty both historically unfounded and ironically humorless.

Chesterton meditates on an anthology of bad verse, distinguishing hopeless non-poets from great poets who fail precisely when most faithful to their own fashionable style, concluding that Carlylean hero-worship — whitewashing poets as gods — corrupts honest critical judgment.

Chesterton argues that while progressives once championed positive morality over mere prohibition, modern satirists like Huxley and Lewis can only tear down without offering any positive vision, making them paradoxically kin to the Puritan negativists they replaced.

Chesterton reassesses Jonathan Swift's growing greatness, defends his Tory politics and satirical courage, debunks the trivializing literary legend of his broomstick essay, and argues Swift's genius was negative wisdom—contempt for folly—rather than poetic charity or mystical sight.

Chesterton defends Humanism against opponents who brand it merely "Critical," arguing through Shakespeare's Macbeth that genuine creative art is inseparable from moral judgment and that true creativity requires the artist to share a decisive ethical stance.

Chesterton satirically proposes a tax on superficial name-dropping—particularly invoking Einstein without comprehension—arguing it would curb intellectual posturing and force writers and speakers toward genuine understanding.

Chesterton argues that sound and sense in poetry are inextricably fused — using Milton's line "Like Teneriffe or Atlas unremoved" as proof — and condemns modern poets for seeking to divorce them rather than renew their ancient wedding.

Chesterton argues that literary cliques harm culture by enabling poets to leave work incomplete and deliberately obscure, substituting insider interpretation for the true literary labor of translating inner experience into plain, universally accessible language.

Chesterton argues, contrary to common assumption, that Asia is defined by stark directness and lacks real mystery, while the true cosmic enigma is Western Christian culture with its paradoxical blend of contradictory ideals and layers of self-deception.

Chesterton recounts debating communist writer Middleton Murry and argues against his fatalism, insisting historical events always harbored real alternatives and that human free choice is more fundamental than any doctrine of Necessity.

Chesterton uses a highbrow magazine competition imagining St. George interviewed by a modern journalist to argue that patchily educated moderns miss the real joke: the late Roman Empire under Diocletian was nearly identical to contemporary society in its feminism-for-publicity, proliferating new religions, materialism, and spiritual decay — so the martyred soldier George would feel entirely at home, and prepare again for death.

Chesterton dissects a recurring newspaper article that claims the Good Old Times were bad, arguing it attacks a straw man, picks the worst possible historical period for comparison, and — blinded by faith in modernity — cannot see new evils like universal conscription and state-controlled education.

Chesterton argues that democracy's apparent failure is not democracy's fault but the result of industrialism, capitalism, and modernity creating conditions too indirect and complex for simple popular self-governance to survive.

Chesterton debunks journalistic literalism about Gray's composition of the Elegy, reconstructs a plausible gradual creative process, then links the poem to the twilight passage from Classicism to Romanticism and laments the erosion of English gentry culture that once preserved rural tradition.

Chesterton lampoons evolutionary educators who, unlike even the most bizarre primitive religionists, kill human wonder by reducing all mystery — modesty, beauty, ornament — to flat materialist slogans, leaving minds frozen like statues in a wizard's garden.

Chesterton refutes Spengler's "Decline of the West" by asserting Western civilisation has never broken its thread from Greeks to moderns, then warns that contemporary media-driven amnesia may actually produce the discontinuity Spengler falsely diagnosed in the past.

Chesterton surveys Arthur Bryant's biography of Charles II, arguing that historians underestimate his exceptional intellect—not mere wit but strategic genius—evidenced by his masterful political survival against brilliant opponents during the Popish Plot and his achievement of a second Restoration through sheer unflagging intelligence.

Chesterton argues that higher suicide rates in Nordic cultures versus Mediterranean ones arise not from climate but from a difference in mental and spiritual outlook: Christian Latin civilization breeds a combative, positive spirit, while northern Germanic philosophy breeds introspective melancholy and pessimism.

Chesterton argues modern youth's spiritual emptiness stems not from rebelling against Christianity—which they never possessed—but from losing paganism, the inherited human sense that natural things carry divine meaning, leaving them stunted and cut off from wonder.

Chesterton argues that replacing long formal literary genres (epic, tragedy) with brief impressionistic modern verse paradoxically multiplies total literary output, because each piece's shortness removes the natural brake that extended form imposed on writers.

Chesterton argues that modern civilization perpetually inverts its own aims — individualism spawned communal confusion, property worship destroyed privacy, and state schooling is systematically undone by the chaotic world the same state produces around the child.

Chesterton argues that Romanticism was a recent revolutionary movement whose twin ideals — Love and Liberty — were fragments of Christian mysticism torn from their religious ground and thus doomed to collapse, and that every generation's rebellion inevitably fossilises into the old convention the next generation rebels against.

Chesterton argues Chaucer defies modern misconceptions of medievalism by embodying a uniquely sane, cheerful, practically-minded artist whose merry temperament unified worldly duty and lyric poetry without inner conflict.
